To assassinate someone means to deliberately and intentionally kill a person who is important, famous, or powerful — usually for political, religious, or ideological reasons.

It is not just any killing. It is a planned, purposeful murder of a significant public figure. The planning and the status of the victim are what make it an assassination, not just a homicide.
The Three Pillars of This Word

To truly understand "assassinate," remember these three defining features:

1. The victim must be notable.
The target is almost always a person of public importance — a political leader, a head of state, a military commander, a religious figure, a prominent activist, or a public figure of significant influence. You would not use "assassinate" to describe the killing of an ordinary private person. Ordinary people are murdered. Important public figures are assassinated.

2. The killing is planned.
Assassination is never accidental or spontaneous. It is premeditated — thought out in advance. There is intent. Someone decided this person must die, and steps were taken to make it happen.

3. The motive is usually political, ideological, or strategic.
The killer (called an assassin) acts because of what the victim represents or what the victim does, not typically out of a personal grudge. The goal is usually to silence a movement, send a message, shift power, or remove an obstacle.

• "A gunman assassinated the president as he was leaving the building."
  • "The rebel group attempted to assassinate the military general but failed."
  • "Throughout history, many world leaders have been assassinated for their political beliefs."

• It does not mean to kill just anyone. If someone kills their neighbor in a fight, that is murder — not assassination.
  • It does not imply war. Soldiers killing each other on a battlefield is combat. Assassination is targeted and specific.
  • It does not require success. You can attempt to assassinate someone and fail. The intent and act of trying still counts. ("They attempted to assassinate the prime minister.")

"Assassinate" is also used in a non-physical, figurative way in the phrase "assassinate someone's character" (or "character assassination").

This means deliberately destroying someone's reputation — not their body, but their image in the eyes of others. It is done through lies, rumours, false accusations, or deliberate manipulation of facts.

  • "His political opponents tried to assassinate his character by spreading false stories about him."

Just like a physical assassination, character assassination is deliberate, targeted, and meant to destroy. The only difference is that the weapon is words and lies rather than a physical weapon.

Since you'll encounter these forms everywhere, here they are:

  • Assassin (noun) — the person who carries out the assassination. ("The assassin was captured.")
  • Assassination (noun) — the act itself. ("The assassination shocked the entire nation.")
  • Assassinate (verb) — the action. ("They plotted to assassinate the senator.")
  • Assassinated (past tense) — when it already happened. ("The leader was assassinated in 1963.")
The Big Picture — One Line to Remember

To assassinate = to deliberately kill a prominent, important, or powerful person, almost always for political or ideological reasons, as part of a planned act.

If the victim is powerful and the killing is planned and purposeful, the word is "assassinate." Everything else is the ordinary, tragic word: murder.
